Theodore White interviews Mrs. Kennedy at Hyannis Port until 2 AM; his notes, given to the Kennedy Library in 1969, stay sealed until a year after her death in 1994.
Johnson tells Sen. Richard Russell he has already announced him as a commissioner; Russell says Johnson was wrong to pick Warren and him, but he will do his best.

Life publishes selected Zapruder frames. Paris Presse reports the FBI said Oswald had an accomplice at the window. A letter from Oswald to Communist Party official Arnold Johnson, postmarked November 1, arrives four weeks late; Johnson notes oddities in the ink and signature, but no handwriting analysis or postal inquiry follows.
Joseph Campisi visits Ruby in the county jail.
FBI agent Alan Manning records a report that women at a sewing room across from the Depository knew Oswald and Ruby and saw Ruby hand Oswald a pistol.

The wife of a Connecticut relative of Officer Tippit tells the FBI an anonymous, frightened woman called claiming to know Oswald's Hungarian communist "father and uncle" in New York. Robert Kennedy's direct line to Hoover is disconnected on Hoover's orders.
Drew Pearson reports Secret Service agents drank at the Fort Worth Press Club until nearly 3 AM on November 22, some going on to The Cellar. Chief Rowley orders every agent to account for that night.

December 1 had reportedly been set for a Kennedy-authorized "Plan for a Coup in Cuba" (the CIA's AMWORLD program, declassified 1999), abandoned after the assassination. Marina tells the Secret Service she never saw a scoped rifle before the assassination or her husband with a pistol, which conflicts with her taking the backyard photographs.
Manning's report on the sewing-room women is dated today; neither the Warren Commission nor the HSCA appears to follow it up.
Orville Nix gives his film to the FBI, which copies it. Johnson visits Kennedy's grave.

Jean Hill says her boyfriend, motorcycle officer J.B. Marshall, warned her that people who mind their own business live longer, and that FBI chief Shanklin later urged her to alter her account. She says she was followed and her home watched.
Rolando Cubela (AMLASH) returns to Cuba from Prague.

Men identifying themselves as FBI agents take the Dallas Morning News photos of a pool of blood found by Jerry Coley, telling him it never happened. White House photographer Joe O'Donnell later claims Mrs. Kennedy watched the Zapruder film with him and that he cut about ten feet from it. An FBI replica of the paper bag is found to use different paper from the original.
FBI agents in Chicago check Mexicana passenger lists for "Lee Martin" and "Wilfred Oswalt"; they find an "M. Lee," an "R. Martin" and a "J. Oswalt."

Depository worker Frankie Kaiser finds the clipboard Oswald used, with three unfilled orders, hidden on the sixth floor near where the rifle was found, despite earlier searches. Chester Boyers prepares tissue sections from Kennedy's brain. McCone meets Johnson and holds a secret Cuba meeting.
Marina first says Oswald tried to kill General Walker, a week after a German paper suggested a link; the Warren Commission calls that story fabricated but adopts the allegation.

UPI reports the FBI will find Oswald acted alone. Hoover professes surprise, though William Sullivan later says Hoover leaked it to blunt calls for an independent inquiry. Clint Hill receives a Treasury award. Capt. Michael Groves, commander of the funeral honor guard, collapses and dies at dinner at 27; his effects later burn in a fire.
Chief Curry tells Hoover that 196 evidence negatives were not returned; Hoover blames the police photographer's technique.
A Secret Service report quotes Depository worker Harold Norman saying the shots came from directly above him and dust fell from the ceiling; before the Warren Commission he denies saying so.
The FBI returns Nix's film, keeping a copy; Nix is never called as a witness. Measured from his film, the limousine moves more slowly than in Zapruder's.

The FBI collects the Oswalds' remaining things from the Paine house but misses an Imperial Reflex camera. An unstamped package to "Lee Oswald" at a nonexistent address, containing an open paper bag, turns up in the Irving post office; Sylvia Meagher argues whoever sent it was implicated.
The Kennedy infants Patrick and an unnamed daughter are reburied near their father at Arlington.
The New York Times reports that most witnesses stopped helping reporters after FBI interviews.
The Warren Commission meets for the first time, still without the FBI report.
All seven commissioners are never present together for any of the 94 witnesses; Gerald Ford, who reports to Hoover, hears the most, 70.
Bobby Baker later says he and Ford shared access to a lobbyist's hotel suite, offering it as an explanation for Ford's closeness to the FBI.
Katzenbach tells the Commission the leaks of the FBI's conclusions could only have come from the FBI.
Dallas lawyer Carroll Jarnagin writes Hoover that on October 4 he overheard Ruby and a man calling himself H.L. Lee, whom he later recognized as Oswald, discuss killing the Texas governor.
DA Wade says a polygraph showed Jarnagin was at the club but heard no such conversation.
The Secret Service stages the first reenactment, with surveyor Robert West; the plat becomes Exhibit 585, which counsel introduces "not for the truth of the measurements."
Mrs. Kennedy and the children leave the White House.
Life's Paul Mandel writes that the film shows Kennedy turning far right, exposing his throat to the sniper's nest, which the film does not show.
The ACLU says the Dallas officials' public statements would have denied Oswald any fair trial.
A supplemental examination of Kennedy's brain records 1,500 grams; the brain is reportedly not sectioned.

Former Ruby employee William Abadie tells the FBI Ruby was tied to racketeers and corrupt police. Richard Helms removes CIA officer John Whitten from the Agency's inquiry after Whitten complains that Oswald information is being withheld.

Michel Roux leaves the U.S. at Laredo; some authors argue he therefore cannot have been Souetre. A KGB officer, Col. Pavlotsky, is later quoted claiming his unit concluded a Corsican hit man, possibly Souetre, killed Kennedy; the account is unverified.
The Johnsons move into the White House, a day after Mrs. Kennedy leaves.
The press publishes Oswald's letters to Fair Play for Cuba director V.T. Lee.
A rumor claims Secret Service agents burned autopsy materials.
Robert Oswald finds his brother's Imperial Reflex camera at the Paines' and does not report it. The New York Times reports agents suggested Marina return to the Soviet Union.
Hoover gives Johnson the FBI summary report: Oswald acted alone; the back wound entered at a steep downward angle with no exit and no bullet in the body. The Warren Report later contradicts this.
Robert Kennedy writes McCone about plans for a coup in Cuba.
Katzenbach urges the commissioners to announce at once that Oswald was the lone assassin, two months before the first witness.
Citing a Gallup poll showing most Americans believe in a conspiracy, he proposes a statement that the FBI proved Oswald guilty and found no confederates.
The FBI receives tips from the Netherlands, a seaman and a German informant claiming Madame Nhu and the South Vietnamese government were behind the assassination.
McCone holds a secret Cuba meeting; reports that Oswald visited Havana from Mexico are said to be suppressed.
A Western diplomat claims Che Guevara is under house arrest for plotting against Castro.
Two Dallas officers sent to deliver mail to Mrs. Tippit are each called back or told to wait.
Sorrels and McCann report that no agent was drunk the night before the assassination.

A police memo relays a mechanic's report that Oswald drove Ruby's car; Ruby's known mechanic is never asked. Alma Cole writes Johnson that her son knew Oswald in Stanley, North Dakota, where the boy read communist books and said he was called to kill the President.
An FBI teletype says NBC promised to air only material consistent with the Bureau's report.

The limousine goes to be rebuilt. An FBI envelope labeled "7.65 shell found in Dealey Plaza," marked of no value and destroyed, surfaces only in 1995; early witnesses had called the rifle a 7.65 Mauser.
Hoover writes that he believes Oswald was the assassin but is troubled whether he acted alone, citing unproven letters from Cuba about the "job" and a promised reception by "the chief."

The Commission gains subpoena power. The Dallas Morning News asks whether a bullet chipped the Main Street curb near the underpass, where bystander James Tague was nicked; the FBI interviews Tague the next day.
The curb mark, photographed by Tom Dillard and reported to U.S. Attorney Barefoot Sanders, is later found patched.
Johnson recalls Ambassador Mann, who had been pursuing a Cuban link, and gives him a State Department post.
Rex Basinger, jailed for vagrancy, later tells his brother Ruby spoke in jail of a May 1964 invasion of Cuba.
Marine navigator Larry Huff says he flew military investigators from Hawaii to Japan to research Oswald; the report disappears from Marine files.
At the Commission's second meeting, Sen. Russell tells Allen Dulles he thinks the CIA will "doctor anything they hand us."
The CIA opens a file on Gilberto Policarpo Lopez.
The HSCA later details Lopez's Fair Play for Cuba ties, his Tampa contacts, and his Laredo crossing and Havana flight, and faults the CIA for not pressing the leads or telling the Warren Commission.
Cuban intelligence general Fabián Escalante later asserts that the CIA, the Mafia and Cuban exiles carried out the assassination, naming exile shooters and various CIA and Mafia figures.
Howard Brennan, not wearing his glasses that day, says he is sure the gunman was Oswald; by January 7 he says he cannot be positive.
The Times reports the FBI report places one hit where the shoulder meets the neck and another at the right temple.
Press leaks describe a shallow back wound and say a fragment of the head shot caused the throat wound.
Reporter Richard Dudman says Secret Service agents visited the Parkland surgeons with the autopsy report, after which they revised their view of the throat wound.
A Times report says the back bullet lodged in the body and a fragment from the head shot exited the neck; weeks later the Times still says a bullet lodged in the shoulder.
The FBI interviews Silvia Odio about a visit by "Leon" with two Cubans. FBI work in New Orleans ends; its January report omits Ferrie and Marcello.
UPI reports the limousine is being armored at Ford in Dearborn with a new windshield.
At his first major National Security Council meeting, without Robert Kennedy, Johnson signals caution on Cuba.
The Secret Service sends the autopsy report to the Commission, and the limousine is released for rebuilding ("Quick Fix").
Hoover notes 1959 press reports that Oswald said he had lived in North Dakota; Alma Cole's letter reached the FBI December 19.

McNamara recommends deeper involvement in Vietnam. Reporter Richard Dudman writes that he and others saw a hole in the limousine windshield at Parkland; motorcycle officers H.R. Freeman and Stavis Ellis later describe a bullet hole as well.
The FBI interviews Ruby a second time.

Harry Truman writes in the Washington Post that the CIA has strayed from intelligence into operations and policy and needs to be reined in. Agents adjust to Johnson's volatile temper; rumors spread that the FBI may take over presidential protection.
The FBI and the Commission receive the official autopsy report.
Johnson reportedly tells the Joint Chiefs at a reception, "Just let me get elected, and then you can have your war."
Mrs. Kennedy and the children spend Christmas in Palm Beach.

Life's Mandel article claims the film shows Kennedy turned toward the sniper's nest when hit in the throat. Che Guevara appears on Cuban TV. Johnson goes to his ranch; tensions grow between his agents and former Kennedy detail agents.
Mrs. Earle Cabell testifies that on New Year's Eve a caller told her, "We are coming to kill that Goddamn mayor now."
Theodore White later describes Johnson in these months as harsh to staff and drinking heavily.
Nixon and advisers agree he should lie low but stay available as a compromise candidate.
A medical journal reports a bullet removed from deep in Kennedy's shoulder at autopsy.
Wade says there is no evidence of collusion between Ruby and Dallas police.
Rowley tells Rankin the limousine's blood was cleaned on November 24 because of the smell.
Agent Geis suggests the windshield-trim dent predated Dallas; the garage manager cannot confirm it. By now the car is being rebuilt with armor and a permanent top, and the trim is likely gone.
The FBI bugs Martin Luther King's Washington hotel room; Hoover reacts with contempt to the recordings (per Hersh, Bobby and J. Edgar).
William Sullivan later says Hoover arranged the anonymous package of tapes and a letter urging King to kill himself, which reached the Kings in late 1964 after his Nobel Prize.
Brennan again tells the FBI he cannot positively identify Oswald.
Journalist Lisa Howard, a back channel to Castro, dies in 1965, an apparent suicide.
Robert Kennedy writes Allen Dulles that much of the administration's important material was never written down.
Robert Kennedy returns to work; the FBI stops sending a car for him.
Ruby's second bail hearing is postponed.
J. Lee Rankin tells the Times the Commission aims to show the world the U.S. can protect its President and treat the accused fairly.
Johnson publicly thanks Robert Kennedy for his campaign against the Mafia.
An FBI report repeats the wound description it knew by December 23 to be wrong.
Hoover concedes the first police description of the suspect came from an unidentified citizen who saw someone resembling Oswald run from the Depository.
Rankin asks Hoover for the photographic evidence; Hoover complies.
A Secret Service agent questions Marina for two hours about Richard Case Nagell.

KGB officer Yuri Nosenko defects, saying he handled Oswald's case and the KGB never used him. The CIA holds him in solitary for over three years; he fails polygraphs but holds to his story. Hoover blocks the CIA from putting its Oswald questions to him.

Warren tells staff Johnson said rumors, including that a faction within the government wanted Johnson in power, could lead to a war costing forty million lives, and that circumstances had to override principle.
At Ruby's second bail hearing the judge orders neurological tests and Melvin Belli withdraws the bail motion. Jimmy Hoffa's jury-tampering trial opens in Chattanooga.
In secret session, the Commission worries Marina may testify Oswald was a Soviet agent; Russell says that would "blow the lid."
